title: About me
body:
Why MageTech?

One of my first email addresses was randomly assigned as MagE01@****.com

Also, being a bit of sci-fi nerd I remembered the Arthur C. Clarke quote ,"Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic"...I may have been a bit full of myself in the early years.

I never developed a portfolio or Git repo because I've been too busy writing code that makes money for companies. This updated website is an effort to change that, it was built with AI. Read the next post to learn more!

title: Built with AI
body:
Am I a good developer because I am lazy? Maybe. I’ve stayed gainfully employed through a couple of recessions so that says something I guess.

But I admit I have been feeling the heat from the AI revolution. So this website is an experiment in being as vibe codey as possible. I’ve been using Junie from IntelliJ and chatGPT (Cat, I farted for you French speakers).

I’ve posted the code at a Git repo.

title: The job interview
body:
I've done a low-tech screen recording of a personal code review of the current state of the project.

This will give you an idea of my thought process and how I conduct myself in an interview.

If you are looking for someone who can calculate a Fibonacci sequence using recursive calls during a job interview without the use of StackOverflow/Google/AI, I'm not your developer.

If you are looking for an experienced, thoughtful developer who is capable of getting stuff done in short order, please say hello. :)

title: HIPAA compliant chatbot in 8 hours....sorta
body:
Here is a chatbot that I built in 8 hours using AI. It tries to be HIPAA compliant.

It uses Telegram bot for a secure channel. On my local machine, the text file is encrypted as is my hard-drive. So the spirit is there.

NestJS is the backend. It handles appending messages to an encrypted file.

It is meant as an answering service for a therapist. It is not meant to provide treatment but to provide a high-level summary of a client's messages sent to bot.

For this POC, I used an Ollama local server using llama3.2. Here's a git repo with more details: https://github.com/emaggini-1/nestjs-telegram-bot.git

title: AI Coding Evolution: 6 Months Later
body:
Six months have passed since my last post about AI coding tools, and the pace of change has been nothing short of remarkable. What was revolutionary then is now table stakes, and the bar keeps rising.

Discoveries from Band Fan Site Development

I've been developing a band fan site with NFT claiming functionality, and AI tools have been instrumental throughout. Here are some key discoveries:

1. Dependency Compatibility Issues

The project ran into Angular 21 compatibility issues with @heavy-duty/wallet-adapter. AI tools helped me quickly identify the problem and pivot to using @solana/wallet-adapter-phantom directly with a custom WalletService using Angular signals. This saved hours of debugging and research.

2. Comprehensive Code Reviews

I ran an AI-assisted code review that uncovered 8 issues ranging from high to low severity, including unimplemented NFT claim flows, missing routes, and type safety bypasses in critical wallet paths. The AI not only found these issues but provided actionable recommendations with specific file references and line numbers.

3. Implementation Planning

AI helped me create a detailed 20-step implementation plan covering MVP through production hardening. The plan includes specific verification checklists for each step, making it easy to track progress and ensure nothing is missed.

4. Documentation Generation

The Phantom wallet setup guide was largely generated by AI, with step-by-step instructions for connecting the wallet using Brave browser. The AI anticipated common troubleshooting scenarios and included solutions.

Editor's note: The entirety of this update was done with the prompt:
This project uses ~/IdeaProjects/magetech-ai-vibe/src/assets/blog-posts.json as the source for the posts.

1) create a new branch
2) write an update about how much has change in the AI assisted coding space in the past 6 months.
3) include my personal discoveries in developing ~/dev/band-fan-site

Band fan site contains breadcrumbs which helped with context.

title: What I learned building a RAG chatbot for a 1,104-page manual
body:
I'm a Digital Performer user. For the uninitiated, Digital Performer is MOTU's professional DAW — powerful, deep, and blessed with a user guide that is over a thousand pages long. When I want to know how to do something, I want an answer in five seconds, not five minutes of PDF scrolling. So I built a chatbot.

The pattern is called RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Instead of asking an LLM to remember the manual (it can't — it was never trained on it), you embed the manual as vectors, embed the user's question the same way, find the closest passages with a similarity search, and hand those passages to the LLM as context. The LLM reads them and synthesises an answer. It doesn't need to "know" anything — it just needs to be good at reading English and following instructions.

The pipeline

Before the chatbot can run, you have to build the index. The process is humbling in how mechanical it is:

  1. Extract — PyMuPDF pulls text from the PDF page by page.
  2. Clean — OCR'd PDFs are full of garbage: soft hyphens (\u00ad), fi/fl ligatures that become garbled characters, lines that hyphenate mid-word across a line break. A handful of regex substitutions fix most of it.
  3. Chunk — The full text is split into 512-token segments with a 100-token overlap. The overlap means a sentence split across a boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk. I used tiktoken to count tokens so the chunks match what GPT-4o-mini will actually see.
  4. Embed — Each chunk is turned into a 384-dimensional vector using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a sentence-transformers model that runs entirely locally. 1,550 chunks in total.
  5. Deduplicate — MinHash LSH catches near-duplicate chunks (the manual has plenty of repeated boilerplate). Running dedup before building the index means the LLM doesn't see the same text twice.

Why local embeddings?

This was the first thing that surprised me. You must embed queries with the same model you used to embed the documents. If you index with model A and query with model B, the vectors live in different geometric spaces and the similarity scores are meaningless. Since I embedded the manual offline with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, every live query has to go through that same model too. Running it locally adds about 10ms per query, costs nothing, and keeps the two embedding spaces in sync. Using the OpenAI embeddings API at query time would break everything.

The search is just a similarity race

When you ask the chatbot a question, the system needs to find which of the 1,550 text chunks is most relevant to your question. Both the question and every chunk have already been converted into lists of 384 numbers — think of each list as a GPS coordinate, except instead of two dimensions (latitude, longitude) there are 384. Similar meaning = coordinates that are close together in that space.

Finding the closest chunks is then just arithmetic: compare your question's coordinates against every chunk's coordinates and rank them by closeness. That sounds slow, but it isn't. All 1,550 sets of coordinates are stored side-by-side in memory, and a single highly-optimised library call compares them all simultaneously rather than one at a time. The whole search finishes in under a millisecond — faster than your browser can blink.

One small trick that makes this work cleanly: before storing the coordinates, each one is rescaled so it sits exactly on the surface of an imaginary sphere. Once everything is on the same sphere, measuring “closeness” simplifies from a more complex formula down to a single multiplication step per chunk. Doing that rescaling once at index time (rather than every time someone asks a question) is what keeps live queries fast.

Constraint prompting kills hallucination

The system prompt tells the LLM: "Answer using ONLY the User Guide excerpts provided below." This single instruction is doing a lot of work. Without it, the model freely blends the retrieved text with things it half-remembers from training — and Digital Performer is niche enough that its training data was probably sparse and unreliable. With the constraint, the model treats the retrieved chunks as the authoritative source and its job becomes synthesis and citation rather than recall. Temperature is set to 0.2 to keep answers consistent and factual.

Clickable page citations were a nice touch. The LLM is instructed to embed [page X] markers in its answer; a JavaScript regex on the frontend replaces them with hyperlinks pointing into the PDF using the #page=N fragment identifier. The browser's native PDF viewer handles the rest.

What REALLY surprised me

The chunking strategy matters more than the model choice. I initially chunked at 256 tokens without overlap and got retrieval failures on questions whose answer spanned two chunks. Increasing to 512 tokens with 100-token overlap fixed most of them. The LLM is not the bottleneck — retrieval quality is.

OCR cleaning also matters more than you'd expect. Some PDFs store certain letter pairs — like fl, fi, or ff — as a single fused glyph called a ligature. It looks identical on screen, but under the hood the word “workflow” might be stored as a three-character sequence where the last two letters are a single private Unicode character rather than an f followed by an l. When someone types “workflow” into the search box, the query vector and the garbled index vector end up pointing in completely different directions — the match fails silently. The cleaning step is boring but load-bearing.

The whole thing runs for about $0.001–0.003 per query using GPT-4o-mini. For occasional personal use that's essentially free. There's also an Ollama path wired in — swap the base URL and you get fully local inference with no API key needed, just slower answers.

The code is on GitHub if you want to adapt it to any large document.
